confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hotz Molina, Rolf Stephan. 2025. A grammar of Tawrã Mishmi. PhD thesis, University of Sydney. 659 pp. hdl:2123/34036 (Sydney eScholarship, open-access).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.2.6 'Tone and metrical structure: tonal patterns', pp. 82-84, Table 2.21 p. 83, Table 2.22 p. 84; cross-checked: overview p. 62, sec. 2.2.1 p. 63 (heavy vs light syllable), sec. 2.2.2 p. 67 (H.H trochaic words), sec. 2.5.5 p. 147, sec. 2.5.6 p. 152.
catalog_quote: the overall stress system can be defined thus: Stress falls of the first heavy syllable from left to right. The weight of a syllable is lexically determined and does not change. Stress on the initial syllable (trochaic pattern) will define a syllable as heavy. [p. 82] ... On the contrary, in an iambic pattern, the first syllable is light and the stress falls on the second, heavy syllable. [p. 83] ... Tawrã falls into the second group of languages where stress is unpredictable (free stress languages) as evidenced by a number of stressed-based minimal pairs. Table 2.22 displays three segmental minimal pairs based solely on stress (and disregarding tonal differences). The first column from left to right has words with the stress falling on the initial syllable (trochaic foot type) while the second column has words with tone on the second syllable (iambic foot type) ... As a general tendency, iambic words are much more common than trochaic words in the language. ... the phonological correlation of stress/accentuated syllable in Tawrã cannot be teased apart from the effect of tone since pitch, intensity and duration are also features of the individual tonemes ... in other words, there is an isomorphism between the tone-bearing unit (henceforth TBU) and stress. [p. 84]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tonal language (four tones) in which the phonological word has exactly one heavy syllable that carries both the single word stress and the single tone (stress and tone-bearing unit are isomorphic). Disyllabic words are lexically either iambic (stress and tone on the second/final syllable; the common case, all four tones possible) or trochaic (stress on the first syllable; only high-falling+mid pattern). Formally 'stress falls on the first heavy syllable from the left', but syllable weight is lexical and in trochaic words is diagnosed by the stress itself, so placement is unpredictable and there are stress-based minimal pairs (e.g. 'hâ.wa 'make sound' vs ha.'wa 'delay').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described: only one (primary/main) stress per phonological word; light syllables are unfooted, toneless grammatical suffixes and clitics carry no stress (p. 83 fn. 10; sec. 2.2.5).
new_statements.exceptions: H.H trochaic words stress only the initial syllable (p. 67); native trisyllables are very rare (mostly old compounds) and have stress on the first or second syllable with three tonal patterns, no stress-based minimal pairs (sec. 2.5.6, p. 152); words longer than three syllables unattested; author notes phonetic cues of stress cannot be separated from those of tone (p. 84).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('the tone- and stress-bearing unit is the word', abstract); compounds may contain more than one phonological word, each with its own stress/tone; data from citation forms and field recordings of speakers from Lohit and Anjaw districts, Arunachal Pradesh (2022-2024).
new_statements.identity_note: Hotz 2025 describes Tawrã as spoken in Lohit and Anjaw districts, Arunachal Pradesh, India (speakers BT, JO etc.), i.e. the Indian-side variety of diga1241 (Digaru/Taraon); the Chinese-side variety (Darang Deng of Chayu, Tibet) is the object of Jiang et al. 2013 and Zong 2019, same glottocode. Sastry 1984 'Mishmi Grammar' is also Digaru/Taraon (not Idu or Kman).

tone_statements.citation: Evans, Jonathan P. & Johakso Manyu. 2021. The sounds of Tawrã (Digaru-Mishmi), a Tibeto-Burman language. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 44(1): 1-26.
tone_statements.quote: Tawrã, like numerous Tibeto-Burman languages of Northeast India, has up to one tone per lexical morpheme, which can consist of more than one syllable (Morey 2008; Post 2015). Tawrã tonal phenomena can be described with reference to three tonemes, H(igh), L(ow) and HL (falling). Not every morpheme has a specified tone. If no tone is assigned to a syllable (Ø), then it receives a default M(id) pitch. ... The Mid pitch assignment itself is not a toneme.
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes H, L, HL (falling), max one per lexical morpheme (TBU = morpheme per source); toneless morphemes/syllables surface Mid, not a toneme. F0 plots; HL's L may land on the next syllable.

Unpublished working paper 'circulated for comment', Kay Williamson Educational Foundation, Cambridge; revised version of a lecture presented to CALSOM (Cultural and Literary Society of Mishmi), 6 March 2015. 12 pp. Posted on academia.edu, document 12868198 (uploaded 8 June 2015).
tone_statements.quote: Tawra has at least two level tones, high and non-high, as well as a rising and a rare falling tone. There are four possible tones on a single syllable. These are marked as follows; Low ... High ... Rising ... Falling ... A typical example of a minimal pair is as follows; beak lá tooth lá Tawra tones can be dynamic in compounds. For example, the word mustard tủ has a rising tone in isolation. However, when combined in the word mustard oil túcây it loses the rising tone [which probably spreads rightwards] and the second syllable gains a falling tone.
tone_statements.summary: Four tones per syllable: low (commonest), high, rising, rare falling; tones change in compounds. Text copy lost diacritics: mark table shows dots, beak/tooth both print 'lá' (3.3 writes lá vs la).
